title: The Last Copper Plate of Vallabhi

title_i18n.en: The Last Copper Plate of Vallabhi

subtitle: When History Falls Silent at Vallabhi’s Gate
era: End of Maitraka rule, c. 762-776 CE

sources.citation: Last known copper-plate grant of Siladitya VI Dhruvatta, c. 776 CE
sources.note: Final administrative marker for the Maitraka line.

sources.citation: Dhaneshwara, Shatrunjaya-Mahatmaya; Charan and Khodiyar traditions
sources.note: Later religious and bardic memories linking Vallabhi's fall to invasion and local sacred memory.

sources.citation: R. C. Majumdar, The History and Culture of the Indian People, Vol. III (1954); Virji, The Later Guptas (1955)
sources.note: Modern scholarship emphasizing that no historical source records exactly how the dynasty ended.

panels.shot: epic low-angle wide of a king before a vast, shadowed archive

dialogue.text: In Vallabhi’s last copper plate, c. 776 CE, Siladitya VI speaks clearly—then, without warning, the Maitraka kingdom vanishes into silence.

panels.shot: slow push-in from cityscape to palace interior

dialogue.text: For two centuries Vallabhi in Saurashtra had spoken in copper and palm leaf, its Maitraka rulers recording grants and lineages in steady, royal prose.

panels.shot: medium shot over a scribe’s shoulder

dialogue.text: In the reign of Siladitya VI Dhruvatta, around 776 CE, one such grant was ordered—the last Maitraka copper plate known to survive.

panels.shot: extreme close-up of the copper plate surface

dialogue.text: Its language is familiar: royal titles, pious invocations, record of a grant—nothing in its careful letters hints that the line is about to end.

panels.shot: wide shot of the record office hall

dialogue.text: Behind that plate lies an entire archival world—earlier Siladityas, grants to Brahmins and temples, the slow spread of Maitraka authority across Gujarat.

panels.shot: high-angle shot looking down on the king and map

dialogue.text: By the mid‑8th century, powers shifted around Vallabhi—the rise of new dynasties in western India, the presence of Arab forces along the Sindh and coastal routes.
Later Jain and local traditions would speak of Tajjika—Arab—attack and destruction, tying Vallabhi’s fall to the sea‑facing horizon Siladitya VI once watched.

panels.shot: cut to later-era devotional scene, slightly desaturated

dialogue.text: Texts like the Shatrunjaya‑Mahatmaya, and Charan and Khodiyar traditions, fold Vallabhi’s end into sacred memory—where invasion, gods, and loss share the same story.

panels.shot: slow fade between inscription and listening crowd

dialogue.text: But the copper plate of c. 776 itself is silent about catastrophe. It records a grant, not a siege, and names no foreign captor at Vallabhi’s gate.

dialogue.speaker: siladitya_vi_dhruvatta
dialogue.text: Ensure this stands among our line. Let it be kept well.

panels.shot: symbolic shot of the plate being stored

dialogue.text: It is stored as countless charters before it were, one more official voice in the Maitraka record—yet from our vantage, it stands as the final word.
After Siladitya VI’s last known grant, the archive falls quiet. No dated Maitraka plates follow, no fresh royal names step clearly from stone or copper.

panels.shot: scholarly interior shot with books and inscriptions

dialogue.text: R. C. Majumdar and Virji, reading every trace, warn plainly: no surviving historical source tells us exactly how the Maitraka dynasty came to its end.

panels.shot: split composition contrasting legend and evidence

dialogue.text: Legend paints sieges, burnings, and heroics. The record, by contrast, simply stops—forcing us to separate faith and folklore from what the evidence can bear.

panels.shot: close-up on a scholar’s hand underlining text

dialogue.text: From that final inscription date, c. 776, historians work backward and outward, mapping alliances and pressures—but no one can honestly script Vallabhi’s last day.

panels.shot: dreamlike shot blending past and present

dialogue.text: Siladitya VI Dhruvatta stands at the edge of our knowledge—his last grant firm and dated, his fate and that of his city left unwritten by his own time.
Honesty begins where evidence ends: in Vallabhi’s silence, we remember that a responsible history sometimes stops at the edge of a mystery and stays there.
